question: Does the asymmetry of the env's arcs (means over the 10 values far from 0) give the best linear rule its edge over naive Bayes, through a net bias of each observation toward 1 or 0 (John's hypothesis), or does the edge come from the other context being one value shared by all observations (conditioning)?

definitions.world: 1275 test context pairs of the FF nets' world (../world.py, ../gen.make_env), test-pair weights; x_i(r0, r1) = u_i(r0) v_i(r1)
definitions.anova: per bit: c = ubar vbar (net bias), alpha = vbar (u - ubar) (r0 main effect), beta = ubar (v - vbar) (r1 main effect), gamma = (u - ubar)(v - vbar) (interaction); x = c + alpha + beta + gamma exactly
definitions.variant: x' = s_c c + s_a alpha + s_b beta + s_g gamma, p' = sigmoid(x')
definitions.episodes: values uniform, counts n_i ~ Bin(T, p') drawn by binomial-CDF inversion from one uniform per count; same seed -> same values and uniforms across variants and T (paired); 1500 training + 1500 test episodes per pair; seeds 0 and 1 use independent episodes

rules.joint: LSE over the other context of lam = sum_i [n_i x_i - T softplus(x_i)]
rules.naive: sum_i n_i log pbar_i + (T - n_i) log(1 - pbar_i), pbar = mean over the other context of p (env.naive_likelihood)
rules.lin: best linear: [n/T, 1] W fitted per pair by cross-entropy to the joint marginals; solved exactly by per-pair Newton (same optimum as ../test.py's L-BFGS, which stops short at large T)
rules.geo: geometric: mean over the other context of lam

definitions.edge: best linear accuracy - naive accuracy (paired per pair)
definitions.accuracy: argmax accuracy per pair, test-pair weighted mean; SE over pairs = sqrt(G/(G-1) sum_g w_g^2 (a_g - abar)^2)

net_bias_hypothesis.verdict: refuted as the source of the env's edge (one narrow exception)
evidence: Removing the net bias c raises the edge (decoding r0, T = 30) from +.049 to +.092; paired difference +.043 +- .001; r1 and a second seed identical (E1).
Scaling the bias shrinks the edge: +.092 / .070 / .049 / .035 / .044 at s_c = 0 / .5 / 1 / 2 / 3, both seeds within .001 (E2b); every rule loses accuracy at large bias (joint .784 -> .657).
The bias gives naive almost nothing: .438 at s_c = 0, .447 at 1 (+.009); .410 and .350 at 2 and 3 (E2b).

Naive's boost over chance comes from the own main effect alpha = vbar (u - ubar), which exists because the OTHER arc is asymmetric: naive .108 / .294 / .447 / .562 / .637 at s_a = 0 / .5 / 1 / 1.5 / 2 (E2c).
Same tables (same bias), same T = 30: the edge falls from +.049 to 0 as fewer observations share one value of r1 (E5), so bias plus many observations is not enough for any edge.
Exception: with no main effects the bias alone makes a small edge (c + gamma +.019 +- .001 vs gamma only +.000), by bending the interaction into a weak main effect through the sigmoid's curvature.

The requested sanity 'c -> -c equals full by n -> T - n' does not hold and should not: relabeling a bit maps (c, alpha, beta, gamma) to (-c, -alpha, -beta, -gamma). That exact check reproduces the env (edge +.049, joint .766, naive .447); c -> -c alone is a different table set (edge +.109, naive .415, joint .759).

conditioning_explanation.verdict: qualified: right about the cause (the other context is one value shared by all observations), wrong about the linear mechanism (the best linear rule does not use the conditional slopes alpha)
supported: No dependence on the other context (-beta-gamma): naive = joint = .692 exactly, edge 0 (E1).

At fixed tables and T = 30 the edge shrinks monotonically as r1 is redrawn more often: +.049 (one r1 per 150 observations), +.033 (per 50), +.020 (per 25), +.002 (per step of 5), 0 (per observation, where naive is exact); -gamma +.128 -> 0 (E5, two seeds).
The edge is 0 for T <= 5 and grows to +.008 / .029 / .049 / .091 / .137 at T = 10 / 20 / 30 / 60 / 120 while the joint posterior on the true r1 rises .44 -> .92 (E3).
Explicit conditioning works: argmax_r0 lam(r0, r1_hat) reaches .760 with the joint's r1 estimate and .605 with naive's own estimate, vs best linear .496 and joint .765 (E3, T = 30).
refuted: The best linear slope profiles are further from alpha than naive's (RMS .646 vs .254 nats per count at T = 30); regressed on naive and alpha jointly: +1.09 naive - 0.46 alpha (R2 .76); in -gamma, where conditioning gives exactly alpha for every r1: +2.71 naive - 1.81 alpha (E4).

Rules restricted to alpha-shaped slopes lose to naive: .430 (per-bit gains + fitted intercepts) and .371 (alpha exactly + fitted intercepts) vs naive .447 and best linear .496 (env, T = 30); in -gamma alpha exactly gives .394 < naive .407, and per-bit gains on alpha's shape (.491) equal per-bit gains on naive's own shape (.491) (E4).

The edge does not follow r1 identification across tables: -gamma has the larger edge with the less identified r1 (+.128 at posterior .494 vs env +.049 at .689); per pair at T = 30 the correlation is +.22 (E3).
conditioning_explanation.replacement_mechanism: Given r0, the shared r1 pushes all counts of an episode together: their covariance has a term T^2 Cov_r1(p) that naive omits (49.0 vs binomial 4.5 counts^2 per bit at T = 30, env). A linear discriminant with naive's own class means and this covariance ('full-mix LDA') has slope profiles matching the best linear rule's (R2 .84 env / .97 -gamma at T = 30, vs .68 / .75 for alpha) and reproduces the edge: +.114 of +.128 (-gamma), +.127 of +.136 (-c-gamma), +.021 of +.049 (env; +.066 of +.137 at T = 120); across the 10 table variants at T = 30 its gain correlates +.89 with the edge. The linear rule discounts the directions in which the shared r1 moves the counts; it does not condition on r1. With the interaction gamma the push depends on r0, which one covariance cannot capture; the quadratic discriminant with r0-specific covariances reaches .716 (joint .765).

verdict.A_plus_B_plus_I: The part of I that is exactly linear in the counts and free of r1 is its r0 main effect I_0 = mean over r1 of I; naive + I_0 is exactly the geometric rule (max deviation 1e-13, same argmax in 100% of 4000 episodes), which scores .311 < naive .447. I's per-count slopes split exactly into (alpha - naive's slope) + (beta - naive's r1 slope) + gamma. The best linear rule keeps the best linear fit of the whole dropped term log sum_r1 exp(B + I) over the episodes that occur, which E4b shows is mostly a covariance correction, not a fixed piece of I.
